name: Sustained, distinctive narrating voice
instruction: Judge whether the narration maintains one deliberate, recognizable register (specific diction, syntax, and tone appropriate to who is narrating) consistently across the whole piece, versus drifting into a flat, generic, or inconsistent register that could belong to any narrator. HIGH: you could identify this piece from a blind paragraph because of its voice. LOW: the prose reads as interchangeable default 'competent internet fiction' voice, or shifts registers without motivation.

name: Earned Payoff
instruction: Score high when the ending delivers a consequence or reversal prepared by earlier details and changes the reader’s understanding; score low when it is arbitrary, merely announced, or absent.

name: Form That Serves Content
instruction: Score high when the chosen form—poem, log, transcript, dialogue, or other structure—creates meaning, pacing, or limitations essential to the story; score low when formatting is merely decorative or the form could be removed without loss.

name: Prompt enacted through consequence, not recited
instruction: Score 5 when the prompt's proposition is demonstrated by events and their costs, such that the story would still work if the prompt's sentence were never spoken aloud in it. Score 1 when the prompt's sentence (or a close paraphrase) is itself the payoff, or when the story is a tableau of the prompt plus backstory explaining how the tableau came about. Restating the prompt early as a scene-setter is neutral; restating it as the climax is the low end.

name: Causal Escalation
instruction: Score high when each major beat changes the characters’ options and increases pressure toward a consequential climax; score low when events remain static, arrive abruptly, or merely accumulate without changing the situation.

name: Emotional payoff earned by prior stakes-building
instruction: Judge whether the story establishes enough context, character investment, or concrete stakes before asserting a major emotional beat (a death, a danger, a revelation), such that the beat feels dramatized rather than merely announced. HIGH: by the time the emotional claim arrives, the reader has been given real material to feel it with. LOW: a large emotional claim is asserted (stated as fact) without the scene-work needed to make a reader feel its weight.

name: The story refuses to gloss itself
instruction: Score 5 when the emotional point and the joke are both left for the reader to complete, so the last line performs rather than summarizes. Score 1 when the text states its own meaning, names the feeling it has just produced, or explains its own punchline. Ignore whether the meaning is obvious; score only whether the story says it out loud.

name: Embodied Scene Presence
instruction: Score high when setting and emotion are conveyed through specific sensory perceptions, physical behavior, and concrete objects; score low when the story relies mainly on summary or abstract explanation.

name: Earned idea payoff from the premise
instruction: Score 5 when the story works out a genuine implication of its own premise that the reader was not handed -- a mechanism, a paradox, a social logic, an inverted consequence -- and the working-out is legible in the text. Score 1 when the premise is illustrated but never interrogated, so the story ends knowing exactly what it knew at the start.

name: Distinctiveness of central conceit
instruction: Judge whether the story's core idea offers a genuinely surprising angle, combination, or reversal on its prompt, versus executing a familiar genre convention straightforwardly with no distinguishing hook. HIGH: the central idea is one you haven't seen many times before, or combines familiar elements in an unexpected way. LOW: the premise is a stock genre setup (a quest, a diplomatic incident, a fated meeting) executed competently but without any distinguishing twist on the idea itself.

name: Dynamic Power in Relationships
instruction: Score high when dialogue and action reveal changing leverage, mismatched knowledge, dependence, affection, or threat between characters; score low when interactions merely exchange exposition and leave the relationships unchanged.

name: Economy of Explanation
instruction: Score high when the story conveys necessary context through selected details and lets readers infer the rest; score low when it pauses for redundant exposition, technical listing, or explanation that the scene does not need.

name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
instruction: Score 5 when all emotional weight is generated inside the shown text, so a reader with no outside knowledge gets the full effect. Score 1 when the story leans on an existing franchise, an earlier installment, or thread context to supply the feeling or the recognition, and a reader lacking that context loses the point. Note the exception: if the prompt itself names the borrowed material, borrowing is licensed and only the failure to add anything to it counts against the story.

name: Tonal Control
instruction: Score high when humor, horror, sentiment, or absurdity are balanced deliberately and shifts reinforce the story’s premise; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or undermine the emotional effect.

name: Diction precision and internal consistency
instruction: Judge whether word choices are used correctly and consistently, and whether small factual/continuity details (spelling of body parts, repeated invented terms) are handled with control, distinguishing genuine precision from small slips a careful editor would flag. HIGH: word choices are exact and repeatable details stay consistent. LOW: there is a word-choice error (a wrong word used for its sound rather than meaning) or a repeated but unclear/misused term.

name: Character-specific voice
instruction: Score whether diction, rhythm, figurative language, and attitude create a distinctive voice appropriate to the character or narrator. Score high when the voice remains controlled and individualized; score low when it is generic or depends on one repeated verbal gimmick.

name: Beats escalate; the situation becomes irreversible
instruction: Track the story's beats in order and ask whether each one changes the situation. CLEARLY SATISFYING: pressure compounds -- new information, new cost, or a closed-off option at each turn -- so that by the end something cannot be undone. CLEARLY FAILING: the same beat repeats with variation but no increase (a gag performed three or four times at the same intensity), or events occur and leave the world exactly as it was found. A story may be static by design if the stasis is the subject, but then the stasis must be doing work the reader can name.

name: Fresh handling of a familiar trope
instruction: Score high if the story takes a well-worn genre trope (monster under the bed, thought-experiment classroom scene, curse reversal, etc.) and complicates, subverts, or extends it in a way a reader wouldn't already expect. Score low if the trope is executed exactly as genre convention predicts, with no additional turn.

name: Resonant closing image
instruction: Score whether the final line or image crystallizes the story’s central tension and adds meaning beyond simple stopping or surprise. Score high when the ending lingers and echoes earlier material; score low when it is generic, abrupt, or merely a disconnected punchline.

name: Subtextual Character Conflict
instruction: Score high when desires, resentments, loyalties, or fears emerge through behavior and implication as well as dialogue; score low when characters simply announce flat motives or stereotypes.

name: Self-Contained Narrative Payoff
instruction: Score high when the presented text establishes enough context, completes a meaningful arc, and lands on an earned endpoint; score low when it depends on prior installments, promotional framing, moderation text, or an unresolved setup.

name: Sentence-level freshness vs. cliche phrasing
instruction: Score high if sentences contain apt, unexpected imagery or phrasing that couldn't be swapped into any other story. Score low if the prose leans on stock phrases and off-the-shelf genre diction ('dead meat,' 'evil clutches,' 'how dare you').

name: Moral discomfort left standing, not resolved for the reader
instruction: Ask whether the story leaves the reader holding something unpleasant. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the piece commits to a perspective the reader cannot comfortably endorse -- a narrator whose reasoning is coherent and wrong, cruelty rendered without editorial distancing, an ending that refuses to adjudicate -- and does not supply a character or line that tells the reader how to feel. CLEARLY FAILING: the moral is stated, the transgressor is punished or reformed on cue, or a figure of authority appears to articulate the rules and the lesson. Judge refusal to resolve, not shock content: gore or profanity alone satisfies nothing.

name: Selective Sensory Specificity
instruction: Score high when concrete sensory details are distinctive, selective, and reveal character, danger, or setting; score low when details are generic, ornamental, or piled on without function.

name: Earned recontextualization
instruction: Score whether a later revelation meaningfully changes the interpretation of earlier details and is prepared by prior evidence. Score high when the reversal feels inevitable in retrospect; score low when it is merely announced or appended at the end.

name: Agency under constraint
instruction: Score whether the protagonist makes consequential choices despite meaningful limitations, and whether those choices alter the story. Score high when decisions reveal character and carry costs; score low when the protagonist mainly observes events or acts without changing the trajectory.

name: Dramatized Exposition
instruction: Score high when necessary context is revealed through consequential action, conflict, or purposeful dialogue; score low when long explanatory passages delay the scene and could be removed without changing events.

name: Premise-to-Plot Transformation
instruction: Score high when the prompt's unusual element generates specific conflict, choices, and meaning; score low when it is merely mentioned or used as decorative genre dressing.

name: Narrative economy
instruction: Score whether the story spends words on details that advance character, tension, setting, or theme. Score high when repetition and setup are purposeful; score low when boilerplate, promotion, recap, or redundant explanation displaces the story.

name: Premise Explored as Sincere Inquiry
instruction: Score high if the story treats its central conceit as something worth genuinely examining, following its implications into new or uncomfortable territory. Score low if the conceit exists solely to set up a single joke or reveal, after which the story has nothing further to say about it.

name: Concrete sensory specificity
instruction: Score high when physical sensations, objects, spaces, and actions make the scene vivid and particular; score low when settings and reactions remain generic or abstract.

name: Psychological Contradiction
instruction: Score high when a character’s feelings, beliefs, and behavior meaningfully conflict; score low when reactions are emotionally obvious, uniform, or unsupported.

name: Reframing Reveal
instruction: Score high when later information substantially changes the meaning of earlier details; score low when the ending only confirms an obvious twist or supplies a disconnected surprise.

name: Tonal Control Across Shifts
instruction: Score high if the story maintains a coherent emotional/tonal register throughout, and if the tone does shift, the shift is deliberately staged and reinforced (e.g., via refrain, escalation, or framing) so it reads as a controlled effect. Score low if the story lurches between incompatible tones -- e.g., whimsical or cute imagery collides with grim or violent content, or a serious emotional beat is undercut by a jokey aside -- in a way that reads as accidental or unresolved rather than intentional.

name: Substantive Completion
instruction: Score high when the ending leaves the reader with a developed emotional, ethical, or conceptual consequence beyond the initial premise; score low when the piece is only a setup, exposition dump, or single punchline.

name: Implied worldbuilding
instruction: Score high when social rules, institutions, history, or technology are revealed through consequences and specific practices; score low when the world is explained directly without being dramatized.

name: Embodied nonhuman perspective
instruction: Score high when a nonhuman or altered narrator’s perceptions, values, metaphors, and assumptions remain consistently shaped by that condition; score low when the narrator is essentially a human voice wearing a costume.

name: Sustained in-world idiolect in the narration
instruction: Judge whether the narrating voice thinks in the concepts its own world would supply, rather than neutral contemporary author-English draped over a costume. Clearly satisfying: the narrator names things as its culture or species would and the reader must translate ('the Great-Long-Lived', 'the Field After', 'We-The-Small'; an alien officer's log that calls whiskey a 'noxious potion' and humans 'skin-beasts'; an in-universe containment manual with its own dating convention and clinical euphemisms). Clearly failing: narration could be lifted into any other story unchanged, and a demon, a whale, or a gargoyle-keeper perceives and phrases things in default modern idiom, with genre proper nouns supplying all the flavor. Do not credit invented names alone; credit invented frames of reference. Score 1 = fully generic narration, 5 = a self-consistent conceptual vocabulary sustained to the last line.

name: Causal escalation
instruction: Score high when each development follows from earlier choices or revelations and intensifies the central problem; score low when events are merely piled on or summarized without causal pressure.

name: Narrative Economy
instruction: Score high when each paragraph, image, or exchange advances character, conflict, atmosphere, or meaning; score low when the piece is padded with exposition, repetition, or ornamental setup.

name: Story stands alone without external paratext
instruction: Judge whether the story is complete and comprehensible using only the text given, versus depending on embedded links to the author's other posts, references to an ongoing personal saga/continuity, or footer plugs to feel complete or land its appeal. High: no fact needed to understand the story is missing from the text itself. Low: the piece leans on 'this is part of an ongoing saga,' hyperlinked backstory, or a subreddit plug to feel finished.

name: Implicit Worldbuilding
instruction: Score high when institutions, customs, history, and rules emerge through behavior, objects, and constraints rather than explanatory summary; score low when the story supplies lore without dramatizing its consequences.

name: Controlled Repetition and Rhythm
instruction: Score high when repeated words, structures, or images accumulate changing meaning and regulate pace; score low when repetition is accidental, ornamental, or merely redundant.

name: Ending reframes what preceded rather than announcing closure
instruction: Score 0-4 on the final beat. 4 = the last lines send the reader back through the story with changed understanding, using material planted earlier, and the reframing is not stated as a conclusion. 2 = a clean, correct resolution that adds no new reading. 0 = the ending states the moral, the emotion, or the lesson learned, OR introduces a frame in the last line that nothing earlier prepared. Both failures should be scored 0: the announced ending and the arbitrary rug-pull are the same defect, an ending that does not arise from the body of the story.

name: Voice With Control
instruction: Score high when diction, syntax, figurative language, and narrative distance consistently express a distinctive consciousness while serving the scene; score low when voice is generic or consists mainly of a repeated mannerism.

name: Interest built by the story, not borrowed from known material
instruction: Score 0-4. 4 = characters, world, and jokes generate their own specificity; where the piece uses a familiar genre or pre-existing characters (which some prompts explicitly require), it supplies a pressure, perception or consequence those sources do not already supply. 2 = competent use of a known register with one original element. 0 = the piece runs on recognition - stock components assembled in the expected order, or imported characters whose entire charge is pre-existing and whose meeting merely confirms what a reader already knows about each. Do not penalize a crossover or a genre exercise for being one; penalize it for adding nothing.

name: Reaches real closure rather than an excerpt hook
instruction: Judge whether the piece reaches an actual ending -- a beginning, complication, and resolution (even a dark or ambiguous one) contained within the text -- versus functioning as an opening or excerpt of a longer work, ending on a hook, a cliffhanger mid-reveal, or a scene-setting line that promises a story not yet begun. High: something has changed and settled by the final line. Low: the final line exists to launch a story the text doesn't actually contain.

name: Non-Obvious Consequence
instruction: Score high when the premise leads to a surprising consequence or choice that is nevertheless psychologically and causally credible; score low when the story merely lists familiar trope ingredients or performs a shallow inversion.

name: Detail that does work versus decorative inventory
instruction: Score 0-4 on what the concrete particulars accomplish. 4 = the specifics imply expertise, economy, danger or social position that the story never states, and deleting them would cost the reader real knowledge. 2 = accurate detail that establishes setting and no more. 0 = nouns catalogued for texture - brands, furnishings, colours, equipment lists - which could be deleted or substituted without any change to what the reader understands. Test each cluster of detail by asking what the reader now knows that they could not have guessed from the prompt.

name: Compression With Narrative Payoff
instruction: Score high when a short or highly selective story efficiently establishes context, character, movement, and payoff; score low when brevity produces a sketch or when length adds little usable information.

name: Premise as a Causal Engine
instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual premise directly causes characters’ choices, conflicts, and events; score low when it merely decorates an otherwise generic scene.

name: Escalation Through Consequence
instruction: Score high when each development narrows options or creates a harder subsequent problem; score low when events accumulate without materially changing what characters can do.

name: Dialogue With Subtext
instruction: Score high when speakers pursue different immediate aims, avoid stating the central issue directly, and reveal relationships through wording and interruption; score low when dialogue only explains the premise or trades interchangeable quips.

name: Self-Implication in Character Desire
instruction: Score high when a protagonist’s goal exposes their own contradiction, weakness, or complicity; score low when characters simply pursue an externally stated objective.

name: Elaboration beyond the inciting gimmick
instruction: High: the story develops texture, consequence, or a secondary layer beyond the single joke or concept that launched it. Low: once the premise or joke is stated, the rest of the piece merely restates or extends the same beat without adding a new dimension (emotional, thematic, or plot).

name: Causal escalation
instruction: Score high when each major beat logically worsens, complicates, or redirects the preceding problem toward a payoff; score low when incidents are merely appended or resolved without buildup.

name: Self-sufficient: no prior installment, source work or link required
instruction: Ask whether a reader holding only the writing prompt and this text can follow it. Clearly satisfying: every person, relationship and prior event the story leans on is supplied inside the piece. Clearly failing: the story depends on a named source work, an earlier installment, or linked posts to be intelligible - proper nouns and grievances arrive already-loaded, or the text explicitly directs the reader to read something else first. Borrowing a widely known public character is not automatically a failure if the piece supplies what it needs; inheriting a private cast is.

name: Moral complication
instruction: Score whether the story complicates the reader’s moral judgment rather than announcing an easy good-versus-evil position. High scores expose hypocrisy, unintended harm, or defensible motives behind troubling behavior; low scores leave ethical conclusions obvious and unexamined.

name: No mutual-knowledge exposition; information arrives under pressure
instruction: Score how the reader learns what the world is. Clearly satisfying: facts reach the reader because a character needs them, uses them, is hurt by them, or acts on them, and any background is inferable from behaviour. Clearly failing: characters recite to one another facts that both plainly already possess - a policy 'the Ensemble put in place over a century ago', a house rule that the speaker and listener have both lived under for decades - or the narration halts to brief the reader on history it could have shown.

name: Recontextualizing ending
instruction: Score high when the ending meaningfully changes how earlier details are understood or completes a prepared implication; score low when it merely stops, repeats the premise, or adds an arbitrary final line.

name: Functional sensory detail
instruction: Score whether concrete sensory and physical details do more than decorate the scene. High scores use texture, sound, smell, or bodily action to reveal danger, mood, setting, or character; low scores use generic description or clutter with no narrative function.

name: Distinctive character voice
instruction: Score how clearly diction, rhythm, dialogue, and narration distinguish the characters and remain consistent with them. High scores make speakers identifiable without tags; low scores make everyone sound interchangeable or communicate mainly through exposition.

name: Concrete sensory/physical grounding
instruction: High: the story renders action through specific bodily sensation, sound, or physical detail (what a character feels, hears, touches) rather than abstract summary of what happened. Low: events are reported at a summary level ('X happened, then Y happened') without physical texture.

name: At least one invented rule or institution drives the scene
instruction: Ask whether the piece contains a specific practice, economy, law, procedure or custom that is not standard issue for its genre, and whether the scene actually turns on it. Clearly satisfying: an invented rule with consequences, such that removing it would collapse the scene. Clearly failing: the setting is assembled entirely from off-the-shelf furniture - tavern, hooded bandit, witch's curse, ominous mage upstairs, magic healing stream - and the invented material is limited to proper nouns. Judge invention, not exoticism: an invented rule can be mundane.

name: Formal/structural risk that serves the content
instruction: High: the story takes a deliberate risk with form (a found document, an in-universe official register, a dialogue-only scene, verse-like line breaks) and that form does real work for the content. Low: the story uses a default straightforward scene-then-ending shape with no formal experimentation.

name: Psychological contradiction
instruction: Score high when a character’s motives, feelings, or self-image conflict in specific, credible ways; score low when characters have one plainly stated motive with no inner friction.

name: Narrative economy
instruction: Score high when nearly every included detail develops character, setting, tension, or payoff; score low when the piece contains digressions, promotional material, repetition, or ornamental information that does not advance the story.

name: Economy with information density
instruction: Score high when nearly every line advances action, character, atmosphere, or world understanding; score low when passages are removable summary, repetition, or digression.

name: Control of a sustained, distinct narrative voice
instruction: Judge whether the story commits to one narrative voice/register and holds it for the whole piece, versus drifting between incompatible registers. High end: a distinctive voice (ironic, confessional, mythic, etc.) sustained from the first line to the last. Low end: the register shifts unpredictably in a way that reads as uncontrolled rather than intentional.

name: Contradictory inner motives
instruction: Score high when a character has competing motives that appear in thought, behavior, and consequential choices; score low when characters possess only one stated attitude and never meaningfully conflict with themselves.

name: Embodied sensory and physical grounding
instruction: Judge how much the story grounds its events in concrete bodily sensation and physical detail (touch, taste, muscle strain, texture, temperature) rather than staying at the level of dialogue and abstract description. High end: specific, felt physical detail a reader's body can register. Low end: scenes conveyed almost entirely through unadorned dialogue or exposition with no physical anchoring.

name: Adds a proposition the prompt did not supply
instruction: Compare the story against the writing prompt and rate what the writer contributed. HIGH: the story supplies a complication, causal explanation, angle, or emotional claim that is nowhere in the prompt line, and the prompt's own content is treated as the starting position rather than the destination. LOW: the story paraphrases the prompt, arrives at exactly the beat the prompt already implied, and stops; or it ignores the prompt entirely. Score the increment over the prompt, not the story's overall quality.

name: Earned causal payoff
instruction: Score high when earlier details constrain and prepare the ending, making the final turn feel inevitable in retrospect; score low when the ending is arbitrary, disconnected, or merely repeats the premise.

name: Deliberate sentence rhythm
instruction: Score high when repetition, fragmentation, pacing, and sentence length clearly embody viewpoint or tension; score low when choppiness or monotony appears accidental and adds no effect.

name: Ending that resonates rather than merely resolves
instruction: Judge the story's final beat: does it leave an emotional or thematic aftertaste extending past the plot's resolution, or does it simply close the loop the plot opened? High end: the last lines add a note of unresolved feeling, irony, or dread that lingers. Low end: the ending is a clean mechanical payoff (the twist is revealed, the joke lands, the loop closes) with nothing left resonating.

name: Late reveal reframes rather than cancels
instruction: If the story turns near the end, rate what the turn does to everything before it. HIGH: the reveal makes the preceding pages mean more -- earlier details become newly legible, and the stakes that were established remain real. LOW: the reveal declares the preceding events unreal or inconsequential (a dream, a simulation, a training exercise, a gag), so that the tension the reader was carrying is retroactively refunded; or the turn arrives with nothing planted for it. Score stories without a late turn on whether their final movement deepens or merely stops.

name: Fresh concrete specificity
instruction: Score high when unusual, exact details make the story’s world and actions singular beyond the basic prompt; score low when settings, names, imagery, and genre beats could be exchanged with stock alternatives.

name: Conceit enacted rather than announced
instruction: Rate how far the story's central premise and its point reach the reader through events, images, and behavior rather than through a sentence that states them. HIGH (clearly satisfying): a reader can say what the story is about, yet no line in the story says it; the premise is inferable only from what characters do, notice, or fail to notice, and any thematic claim is left for the reader to assemble. LOW (clearly failing): a character or the narrator states the premise or the moral outright, a speech explains the story's own meaning, or the closing lines summarize a point the scenes had already made. MID: the material is dramatized but one line spells it out anyway. Note: stating the situation in the first line as setup is not a failure; the failure is explaining the significance the story has already shown.

name: Disciplined ambiguity
instruction: Score high when uncertainty is deliberately seeded, bounded by evidence, and invites inference; score low when obscurity results from missing information, contradiction, or excessive explanation.

name: Reciprocal relationships
instruction: Score high when relationships contain shared history, unequal desires, mutual influence, and responsive change; score low when supporting characters function only as props, exposition devices, or targets.

name: Prompt-detail payoff
instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual defining detail directly determines a later action, revelation, or ending; score low when that detail is mentioned but never materially matters.

name: Controlled tonal modulation
instruction: Score high when shifts among humor, fear, pathos, or absurdity remain deliberate and deepen the same story; score low when tonal changes feel random or undercut the scene unintentionally.

name: One-line beats that earn their isolation
instruction: This story may set short lines or single sentences off on their own. Judge whether those isolations do dramatic work IN CONTEXT: an isolated line should land a turn, a reveal, a shift of attention, or a beat of silence that the surrounding prose has set up, and the story should return to ordinary paragraphing when nothing is being marked. Score 1.0 when nearly every isolated line is placed where a beat belongs and the effect would be lost if it were folded back into the preceding paragraph. Score 0.5 when some isolations do work and others are arbitrary. Score 0.0 when lines are isolated indiscriminately or habitually, so the breaks mark nothing in particular, AND also 0.0 when the story isolates nothing but plainly needed a beat somewhere. Answer NA only if the story is too short to show any paragraphing pattern. Judge the placement, not the quantity: a story with three well-placed breaks scores higher than one with thirty indiscriminate ones.

name: Revision depth: continuity, economy, and closed setups
instruction:
Read the writing prompt and the story, then judge how much substantive reworking the text shows in its CONTENT. Assess four things:
(a) Continuity -- do established facts hold? Character names, ages, relationships, physical details, locations, the timeline, and who knows what at each point should stay consistent, with no drift or contradiction.
(b) Economy -- is each paragraph doing work? Look for redundant sentences, beats restated in different words, throat-clearing before the story starts, and passages that could be cut with no loss.
(c) Closure of setups -- are objects, details, and promises introduced early actually used, paid off, or deliberately left open, rather than simply dropped and forgotten?
(d) Control of tense and point of view -- is the narrating stance held deliberately, with any shift reading as a choice, rather than as the writer losing track mid-scene?
HIGH = the story reads as if it has been gone over: nothing contradicts itself, little could be cut, what is planted is used, the narrating stance is under control.
LOW = the story reads as a single unrevised pass: internal details drift or contradict, passages repeat or wander, elements are introduced and abandoned, the narrating stance slips without purpose.
EXPLICITLY IGNORE all spelling, punctuation, capitalization, apostrophes, paragraph spacing, and formatting. A story riddled with typos can and should score HIGH here if the four properties above hold; a mechanically flawless story can and should score LOW if they do not. Do not reward ambition, subject matter, genre, length, or prose flourish; judge only (a)-(d). Use only the prompt and the story -- do not speculate about the writer, and do not consider how the story was received.
